--- title: "Model complexity" description: "A model's complexity is how freely it can bend to the data. Each method has its own setting for it, and only for a linear model does counting the parameters measure it: there, even a column of random numbers adds to it." order: 3 categories: [generalisation] --- ## The axis of flexibility [Underfitting and overfitting](underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd) placed models along an axis of flexibility, from too rigid to too flexible, and moved a decision tree along it with one setting. This page looks at the axis itself: the setting that moves each method of the course along it, and the one kind of model for which counting its parameters measures it. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Freedom to fit any data A model's **complexity**, or flexibility, is how freely it can bend to the data it is given. One way to picture it is to count the different sets of data the model could fit closely. A straight line fits only data that lie near a line. A tree with one station in each leaf fits any data at all, even counts drawn at random. When such a model fits the survey closely, that says nothing about the survey, because a close fit was never in doubt. Each method has [hyperparameters](../04-how-algorithms-learn/parameter-estimation.qmd), settings chosen before the fit, that fix how complex it can be. Turning them moves the model along the axis. ::: {.diagram} ![Each method has its own complexity setting. More terms, deeper trees with smaller nodes and more boosting trees make a model more flexible. A larger ridge penalty makes it simpler, and adding trees to a random forest makes it steadier, not more flexible.](img/model-complexity.svg){fig-alt="Five rows, one per method, each with an arrow from simpler on the left to more flexible on the right. Linear and polynomial regression: the terms in the model, from few terms to many terms. Ridge regression: the penalty lambda, from large penalty to small penalty, marked: raising it makes the model simpler. Decision tree: depth and minimum node size, from shallow with large nodes to deep with small nodes. Random forest: the node size of its trees, from large nodes to small nodes, marked: more trees, steadier, not more flexible. Boosting: number of trees, depth and learning rate, from few small trees to many deeper trees. A note says each setting orders models within one method, and counts of parameters do not compare across methods."} ::: Two of these settings are easy to misread. In [ridge regression](../04-how-algorithms-learn/map-and-priors.qmd), raising the penalty makes the model simpler, since it pulls every coefficient towards zero. And the number of trees in a random forest is not a complexity setting at all. [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd) found that adding trees to a forest stops helping but does no harm: each tree is as flexible as before, and averaging more of them steadies the prediction without letting it bend further. Boosting is different, because each new tree fits part of what the trees before it got wrong, so more trees do make it more flexible. ## Counting parameters works for a linear model In a linear model, each term adds one coefficient, and each coefficient gives the fitted surface one more way to bend. Its complexity is close to its number of coefficients. For other methods the count is a poor guide. A forest of 500 trees has thousands of split points, far more than any linear model in the course has coefficients, yet adding more trees does not make it overfit. A ridge model keeps every one of its coefficients, but the penalty stops them moving freely; [Regularisation](regularisation.qmd) returns to this. So complexity is compared within one method, by turning its setting. Between methods, the fair comparison is the error on new data. ## Worked example The data and splits are those of [the previous page](underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd): 20 random splits of the training sites into fitting sites and new sites, with each error averaged over the 20. The test sites are still unused. The model is a linear regression on the four measured inputs: depth, temperature, chlorophyll and salinity. Columns of random numbers are then added to it as extra inputs. Each column holds one number per station, drawn at random, so it belongs to the stations just as a measurement does, but by construction it carries no information about the catch. Each column adds a coefficient, and so, on the count above, a little complexity. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) # 20 random splits of the training sites: fitting sites and new sites splits <- group_mc_cv(train, group = site_id, prop = 0.75, times = 20) measured <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu") # 460 columns of random numbers, one number per training station noise <- matrix(rnorm(nrow(train) * 460), nrow = nrow(train), dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("noise", 1:460))) noise_columns <- bind_cols(select(train, station_id), as_tibble(noise)) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train = survey.iloc[train_rows].reset_index(drop=True) # 20 random splits of the training sites: fitting sites and new sites splitter = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=20, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) splits = list(splitter.split(train, groups=train["site_id"])) measured = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] # 460 columns of random numbers, one number per training station rng = np.random.default_rng(123) noise = pd.DataFrame(rng.standard_normal((len(train), 460)), columns=[f"noise{i}" for i in range(1, 461)]) noise_columns = pd.concat([train[["station_id"]], noise], axis=1) ``` ::: ::: ### Adding columns of random numbers For each split, the regression is fitted with no random columns, then with 5, 10 and on up to 400. The last setting adds as many as the fitting stations allow: one coefficient for every fitting station, counting the intercept. Each fit is scored on the fitting stations, by $R^2$ and by RMSE, and on the new sites by RMSE. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counts <- c(0, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 300, 400, Inf) score_split <- function(s) { fitting <- analysis(s) |> left_join(noise_columns, by = "station_id") new <- assessment(s) |> left_join(noise_columns, by = "station_id") map(counts, \(asked) { # at most one coefficient per fitting station, counting the intercept k <- min(asked, nrow(fitting) - length(measured) - 1) columns <- c("abundance", measured, colnames(noise)[seq_len(k)]) line_recipe <- recipe(abundance ~ ., data = fitting[columns]) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) fitted <- workflow(line_recipe, linear_reg()) |> fit(fitting[columns]) fitted_values <- predict(fitted, fitting)$.pred tibble(asked, noise = k, r_squared = rsq_vec(fitting$abundance, fitted_values), training = rmse_vec(fitting$abundance, fitted_values), average = rmse_vec(new$abundance, rep(mean(fitting$abundance), nrow(new))), new = rmse_vec(new$abundance, predict(fitted, new)$.pred)) }) |> list_rbind() } noise_sweep <- map(splits$splits, score_split) |> list_rbind() |> group_by(asked) |> summarise(across(c(noise, r_squared, training, average, new), mean)) |> select(-asked) noise_sweep |> select(-average) |> mutate(noise = round(noise), r_squared = round(r_squared, 3), across(c(training, new), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| noise| r_squared| training| new| |-----:|---------:|--------:|------:| | 0| 0.177| 4.54| 4.56| | 5| 0.180| 4.53| 4.60| | 10| 0.185| 4.52| 4.66| | 25| 0.208| 4.45| 4.73| | 50| 0.256| 4.32| 4.85| | 100| 0.343| 4.06| 5.20| | 200| 0.512| 3.49| 6.41| | 300| 0.710| 2.69| 7.91| | 400| 0.910| 1.50| 14.71| | 443| 1.000| 0.00| 221.52|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} counts = [0, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 300, 400, np.inf] rows = [] for fitting_rows, new_rows in splits: fitting = train.iloc[fitting_rows].merge(noise_columns, on="station_id") new = train.iloc[new_rows].merge(noise_columns, on="station_id") for asked in counts: # at most one coefficient per fitting station, counting the intercept k = int(min(asked, len(fitting) - len(measured) - 1)) columns = measured + [f"noise{i}" for i in range(1, k + 1)] model = Pipeline([("recipe", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("model", LinearRegression())]) fitted = model.fit(fitting[columns], fitting["abundance"]) fitted_values = fitted.predict(fitting[columns]) rows.append({ "asked": asked, "noise": k, "r_squared": r2_score(fitting["abundance"], fitted_values), "training": root_mean_squared_error(fitting["abundance"], fitted_values), "new": root_mean_squared_error(new["abundance"], fitted.predict(new[columns])), }) noise_sweep = (pd.DataFrame(rows).groupby("asked", as_index=False).mean() .drop(columns="asked")) noise_sweep.round({"noise": 0, "r_squared": 3, "training": 2, "new": 2}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | noise | r_squared | training | new | |--------:|------------:|-----------:|-------:| | 0 | 0.121 | 4.11 | 4.31 | | 5 | 0.13 | 4.09 | 4.33 | | 10 | 0.135 | 4.08 | 4.35 | | 25 | 0.172 | 3.99 | 4.42 | | 50 | 0.223 | 3.87 | 4.51 | | 100 | 0.32 | 3.62 | 4.86 | | 200 | 0.517 | 3.05 | 5.82 | | 300 | 0.728 | 2.28 | 7.74 | | 400 | 0.943 | 1.03 | 17.59 | | 428 | 1 | 0 | 191.81 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} breaks <- c(0, 25, 100, 200, 300, 400) fit_panel <- ggplot(noise_sweep, aes(noise, r_squared)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = ml_palette[["blue"]]) + geom_point(size = 2, colour = ml_palette[["blue"]]) + scale_x_sqrt(breaks = breaks) + labs(x = NULL, y = "R², fitting stations", title = "The fit to the fitting stations only improves") new_panel <- ggplot(noise_sweep, aes(noise, new)) + geom_hline(yintercept = baseline, linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]) + geom_point(size = 2, colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]) + annotate("text", x = 150, y = baseline / 1.18, label = "predict the average", hjust = 0, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], size = 3.4) + scale_x_sqrt(breaks = breaks) + scale_y_log10() + labs(x = "Columns of random numbers added", y = "RMSE, new sites", title = "The error on new sites only worsens", subtitle = "Log scale") fit_panel / new_panel ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A linear regression on the four measured inputs, with columns of random numbers added, averaged over 20 splits of the training sites. Above, its R² on the fitting stations. Below, its RMSE on new sites, on a log scale; the dashed line is the error of predicting the fitting stations' average count.](model-complexity_files/figure-html/fig-noise-1.png){#fig-noise fig-alt='Two stacked panels sharing a horizontal axis of random columns added, from 0 to about 443 on a square-root scale. Above, R-squared on the fitting stations rises from 0.18 with no random columns, slowly at first and then steeply, to exactly 1 at the right. Below, on a log scale, RMSE on new sites rises from 4.56 with no random columns, crosses a dashed line at 4.83 for predicting the average at about 50 columns, and climbs ever faster to 221.52 at the right.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: ### Reading the sweep **The fit only improves.** With no random columns, the regression's $R^2$ on the fitting stations is 0.177. Every column added raises it, and with 443 columns, on average, it reaches 1.000. This is not chance: adding a column can never lower $R^2$ on the stations the model was fitted to. The fit could always give the new coefficient a value of zero and do exactly as well as before, so it takes whatever small match with the catch the random numbers happen to offer. A higher $R^2$ after adding an input is therefore no evidence that the input matters. **Every column costs on new sites.** Ten random columns already raise the error on new sites from 4.56 to 4.66. With about 50 columns the regression does worse than predicting the average count, 4.83, and the error climbs ever faster from there. There is no number of useless inputs small enough to be free. **The perfect fit is the worst model.** With one coefficient for every fitting station, the regression passes through every station: its $R^2$ is 1 and its training error 0.00. On new sites its error is 221.52, about 46 times that of predicting the average. It has found nothing; it has simply run out of stations to be wrong about. The damage depends on the number of coefficients set against the number of stations. The same columns fitted to many more stations would leave much less room to fit noise, which is why more data is one of the fixes for overfitting. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A model's complexity is how freely it can bend to the data: how many different sets of data it could fit closely. - Each method has hyperparameters that set its complexity. Raising a ridge penalty makes a model simpler, and adding trees to a random forest makes it steadier, not more flexible. - Only for a linear model does the number of coefficients measure complexity. Across methods, compare the error on new data instead. - $R^2$ on the fitting data never falls when an input is added, even a column of random numbers. It cannot show whether an input is worth having. - On the survey, every random column made the regression worse on new sites, and with one coefficient per fitting station it fitted perfectly and predicted worst of all. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Give each split fewer fitting sites by adding `fitting <- fitting |> filter(site_id %in% sample(unique(site_id), 30))` after the line that sets `fitting`. With fewer stations, how many random columns does it take before the regression does worse than predicting the average? 2. Hold the random columns back with a ridge penalty: replace `linear_reg()` with `linear_reg(penalty = 1, mixture = 0) |> set_engine("glmnet")`. Does $R^2$ on the fitting stations still reach 1, and what happens to the error on new sites?
